_schema.note: Hand-researched dossiers. Orbital elements come from CelesTrak/Space-Track. Costs, purpose, and results are compiled from agency budgets, audits, contracts, mission pages, and peer-reviewed or official science summaries — confidence labeled per figure.

confidence.published: Figure appears in an official budget, audit, contract award or operator statement.
confidence.reported: Widely reported by credible trade press, but not in a primary document.
confidence.estimated: Analyst or press estimate. Treat as an order of magnitude only.
confidence.undisclosed: Operator does not publish this. No credible figure exists.

fields.built: Manufacturer, prime contract award, and when the spacecraft finished assembly.
fields.settled: When it reached its operational orbit/slot and was declared operational — often much later than launch.
fields.costBuild: Cost to design and manufacture the spacecraft.
fields.costLaunch: Cost to place it in orbit.
fields.maintenance: What it currently costs to keep flying, per year.
fields.purpose: Why the spacecraft (or constellation) exists: one-sentence intent, users, key instruments/measures.
fields.results: What it has delivered: headline outcome, dated bullets with sources, and what it still produces today.

satellites.name: International Space Station

built.text: Modules built 1994–2011; Zarya (first module) completed by Khrunichev under Boeing contract in 1997.

settled.text: Permanently crewed from Expedition 1. Assembly complete 2011; final major module Nauka added 2021.

costBuild.note: Total international program cost. NASA's own share was ~$75B through 2013 per the NASA Office of Inspector General.

costLaunch.note: ~42 assembly flights (36 Shuttle at ~$450M–$1.5B each, plus Proton/Soyuz). Launch is the dominant line item inside the $150B.

maintenance.note: ~$1.3B station operations & research, ~$1.8B crew and cargo transport. Roscosmos/ESA/JAXA/CSA spend on top of this.

satellites.status: Operational — retirement planned for 2030–2031 via a controlled deorbit vehicle (SpaceX, $843M contract)
sources: NASA OIG IG-14-031, 'Extending the Operational Life of the ISS Until 2024'
SpaceNews, NASA ISS transition cost briefings

purpose.summary: Provide a continuously crewed laboratory in low Earth orbit for science, technology demonstration, and international cooperation.

results.headline: Longest continuous human presence in space and a workhorse for microgravity research.

bullets.text: Permanently crewed since November 2000 — over 25 years of unbroken habitation.
Thousands of investigations flown; results span protein crystals, combustion, Earth imaging, and human physiology for deep-space flight.
bullets.source: NASA ISS Research Overview / annual reports

bullets.text: Enabled commercial cargo/crew (SpaceX, Northrop, Boeing) and private astronaut missions as a market pathfinder.
bullets.source: NASA Commercial Crew / CRS program summaries

results.stillDoing: Crewed research, Earth observation, tech demos; planned transition to commercial LEO destinations ~2030.

satellites.name: Tiangong Space Station (Tianhe core module)

built.text: Developed under Project 921 Phase 3; Tianhe core module completed 2020.

settled.text: Three-module T-shape completed when Mengtian docked. Continuously crewed since June 2022.

costBuild.note: China does not publish a program cost. Western analyst estimates for the station plus supporting Shenzhou/Tianzhou infrastructure.

costLaunch.note: Long March 5B flights estimated at ~$180M each; three module launches plus regular crew/cargo.

maintenance.note: CMSA does not release an operating budget. Cadence is ~2 crew + 1–2 cargo flights per year.

satellites.status: Operational — expansion to six modules announced

purpose.summary: China’s crewed space station for research, technology, and continuous national human spaceflight.

results.headline: Results dossier not yet researched for this entry.

satellites.name: Hubble Space Telescope

built.text: Approved 1977, mirror ground 1979–1981, spacecraft assembled 1985. Launch delayed 4 years by the Challenger stand-down.

settled.text: Deployed 1990-04-25, but the primary mirror had a 2.2 µm spherical aberration. Only fully operational after the COSTAR corrective optics were installed on servicing mission STS-61 in December 1993.

costBuild.note: Development through launch. Lifetime program cost including 5 Shuttle servicing missions is commonly cited at ~$16B.

costLaunch.note: One dedicated Space Shuttle flight. Five further servicing missions cost roughly $700M–$1.1B each.

maintenance.note: NASA astrophysics operating line for Hubble. No longer serviceable — the Shuttle retired in 2011, and three of six gyroscopes remain; the telescope has flown in reduced one-gyro mode since 2024.

satellites.status: Operational — orbit decaying, reentry expected in the 2030s without a reboost mission
sources: NASA FY budget requests, Astrophysics division

purpose.summary: Observe the universe in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared from above Earth’s atmosphere.

results.headline: Transformed modern astronomy — the public and scientific picture of deep space.

bullets.text: Helped establish accelerating cosmic expansion / dark energy evidence (with ground surveys; 2011 Physics Nobel).
bullets.source: STScI / Nobel Committee Type Ia supernova work

bullets.text: Hubble Ultra Deep Field and successors imaged galaxies within ~400 Myr of the Big Bang.
Still drives ~1,000+ peer-reviewed papers per year decades after launch.

results.stillDoing: Guest-observer program; public archive at MAST (STScI).

satellites.name: Chandra X-ray Observatory

built.text: Selected 1977 as AXAF, descoped 1992, spacecraft completed 1998.

launched.vehicle: Space Shuttle Columbia, STS-93 + Inertial Upper Stage

settled.text: IUS and internal propulsion raised it over five burns into a 64-hour highly elliptical orbit. First light 1999-08-19; science operations declared August 1999.

costBuild.note: Total mission cost through the first years of operation is usually given as ~$2.8B.

costLaunch.note: Dedicated Shuttle flight plus an Inertial Upper Stage. Chandra remains the heaviest payload the Shuttle ever launched.

maintenance.note: NASA's FY2025 request proposed winding Chandra down; the operating budget was cut sharply and the mission's future is reviewed annually.

satellites.status: Operational but budget-threatened — thermal degradation limits observing angles

purpose.summary: Map the high-energy universe in X-rays — black holes, galaxy clusters, supernova remnants.

results.headline: Gold-standard X-ray observatory for black holes, dark matter, and explosive astrophysics.

bullets.text: Resolved structure in galaxy-cluster gas and constrained dark-matter / cosmology via cluster physics.
Imaged jets and accretion near stellar-mass and supermassive black holes with sub-arcsecond resolution.
Decades-long archive remains a primary resource for multi-wavelength astronomy.

results.stillDoing: Guest-observer X-ray observations; archive at the Chandra X-ray Center.

satellites.name: Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope
satellites.operator: NASA · US DOE · France · Germany · Italy · Japan · Sweden

built.text: Instrument built at SLAC; spacecraft integration completed 2007 as GLAST.

settled.text: Two-month commissioning; renamed Fermi on 2008-08-26 and began the all-sky survey.

costBuild.note: Total mission cost including instruments and international contributions.

costLaunch.note: Delta II 7920-H under NASA Launch Services.

maintenance.note: One of NASA's cheaper operating astrophysics missions.

satellites.status: Operational

purpose.summary: All-sky gamma-ray observatory for high-energy transients and the extragalactic background.

results.headline: Results dossier not yet researched for this entry.

satellites.name: XMM-Newton

built.text: ESA Horizon 2000 cornerstone mission; assembly completed 1999.

settled.text: Commissioning and calibration ran through mid-2000; routine science from July 2000.

costBuild.note: ESA program cost at 1999 economic conditions.

costLaunch.note: Dedicated Ariane 5 G.

maintenance.note: ESA extends the mission in ~2-year increments; currently approved through 2026+.

satellites.status: Operational — longest-serving ESA science mission

purpose.summary: ESA’s large X-ray observatory for spectroscopy of black holes, clusters, and stars.

results.headline: Results dossier not yet researched for this entry.

satellites.name: Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory

built.text: NASA MIDEX mission selected 1999; completed 2004.

settled.text: Instrument commissioning completed April 2005; normal gamma-ray burst response operations began.

costBuild.note: MIDEX-class cost cap mission.

costLaunch.note: Delta II 7320.

maintenance.note: Faced a proposed FY2025 termination; reprieved. A 2024–2025 orbital decay problem prompted a commercial reboost study.

satellites.status: Operational — orbit decaying faster than planned

purpose.summary: Rapid multi-wavelength follow-up of gamma-ray bursts and other transients.

results.headline: Results dossier not yet researched for this entry.

satellites.name: NuSTAR

built.text: Small Explorer mission selected 2007; completed 2012.

settled.text: 10-metre mast deployed 2012-06-21; science operations began July 2012.

costBuild.note: SMEX cost class.

costLaunch.note: Pegasus XL.

maintenance.note: Among the lowest operating costs of any NASA observatory.

satellites.status: Operational

purpose.summary: Focusing hard X-ray telescope for black holes, supernovae, and compact objects.

results.headline: Results dossier not yet researched for this entry.

satellites.name: Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer

built.text: SMEX selected 2017; spacecraft completed 2021.

settled.text: Boom deployed and commissioning completed; science operations began January 2022.

costBuild.note: NASA cost cap; ASI contributed the detector units separately.

costLaunch.note: NASA Launch Services contract with SpaceX, awarded 2019 — an unusually cheap dedicated Falcon 9 for a small payload.

satellites.status: Operational
sources: NASA Launch Services Program contract announcement, 2019

purpose.summary: Measure X-ray polarization to probe magnetic fields near compact objects.

results.headline: Results dossier not yet researched for this entry.

satellites.name: Terra (EOS AM-1)

built.text: Flagship of the Earth Observing System; completed 1999.

settled.text: Reached its 705 km sun-synchronous 10:30 a.m. descending node; first MODIS imagery released February 2000.

costBuild.note: Includes five instruments contributed by the US, Japan and Canada.

costLaunch.note: Atlas IIAS.

maintenance.note: Now drifting out of its controlled orbit — NASA stopped maintaining the mean local time in 2020 as fuel ran low.

satellites.status: Operational but drifting — instruments degrading, decommissioning expected ~2026

purpose.summary: Flagship Earth Observing System platform for climate, atmosphere, land, and ocean processes.

results.headline: Built the modern daily global view of land, clouds, fires, and Earth’s radiation budget.

bullets.text: MODIS (shared with Aqua) became the workhorse for fire detection, NDVI, snow cover, and ocean color.
CERES measurements underpin Earth’s energy imbalance and cloud-forcing climate records.
ASTER DEM and thermal products widely used for geology, volcanoes, and urban heat.

results.stillDoing: Continuing climate and disaster-support data products via NASA EOSDIS (aging platform).

satellites.name: Aqua (EOS PM-1)

built.text: Second EOS flagship; completed 2002.

settled.text: Led the 'A-Train' formation at a 1:30 p.m. ascending node after ~7 weeks of orbit raising and checkout.

costBuild.note: Six instruments including MODIS and AIRS.

costLaunch.note: Delta II 7920.

maintenance.note: Left the A-Train in 2022 as fuel depleted; now drifting.

satellites.status: Operational but drifting — passivation planned

purpose.summary: Afternoon Earth Observing System satellite focused on the water cycle and atmosphere.

results.headline: Transformed weather and climate sounding from space via AIRS and complementary sensors.

bullets.text: AIRS hyperspectral soundings improved weather forecast skill and climate humidity records.
bullets.source: NASA AIRS project / NWP impact studies

bullets.text: With Terra MODIS, delivered the long-running global fire and vegetation time series.
AMSR-E (and successors) mapped sea ice and soil moisture for polar and hydrology science.

results.stillDoing: Atmospheric and climate data products; platform past design life but still referenced in climate records.

satellites.name: Landsat 8
satellites.manufacturer: Orbital Sciences (bus) · Ball Aerospace (OLI) · NASA GSFC (TIRS)

built.text: Contract to Orbital Sciences 2008; spacecraft completed 2012.

settled.text: Handed over from NASA to USGS after a 100-day on-orbit checkout; renamed from LDCM to Landsat 8.

costBuild.note: NASA lifecycle cost for the Landsat Data Continuity Mission.

costLaunch.note: Atlas V 401 under NASA Launch Services.

maintenance.note: USGS operates both from EROS, South Dakota. All imagery is free and public.

satellites.status: Operational

purpose.summary: Continue the Landsat record of moderate-resolution land imaging for science, resource management, and climate.

results.headline: Anchor of the world’s longest continuous land-imaging archive — free and open since USGS policy change.

bullets.text: With Landsat 7/9, enables multi-decadal maps of deforestation, crops, glaciers, and cities at 30 m.
Free-data policy (from Landsat 1–8 era) unlocked global applications and commercial analytics markets.
Thermal and OLI bands support water-use, burned-area, and urban heat applications worldwide.

results.stillDoing: Operational land imaging with Landsat 9; data via USGS EarthExplorer / cloud collections.

satellites.name: Landsat 9
satellites.manufacturer: Northrop Grumman (bus) · Ball Aerospace (OLI-2) · NASA GSFC (TIRS-2)

built.text: Approved 2015 as a near-rebuild of Landsat 8; completed 2021.

settled.text: Reached its final orbit 8 days out of phase with Landsat 8, giving the pair a joint 8-day revisit. Declared operational and handed to USGS.

costBuild.note: Total mission cost including launch and 5 years of operations was ~$885M.

costLaunch.note: NASA Launch Services contract with ULA, awarded 2019.

satellites.status: Operational

purpose.summary: Near-twin to Landsat 8 to keep an 8-day revisit and secure the Landsat climate data record.

results.headline: Secures Landsat continuity — paired with Landsat 8 for denser global land observations.

bullets.text: Entered service to replace aging Landsat 7 and maintain cross-calibrated continuity with Landsat 8.
Combined L8+L9 revisit (~8 days) improves crop, disaster, and change-detection products.

results.stillDoing: Operational USGS/NASA land imaging; open data distribution.

satellites.name: ICESat-2

built.text: ATLAS laser altimeter development ran long and drove the cost; spacecraft completed 2018.

launched.vehicle: Delta II 7420-10C — the final Delta II flight ever

settled.text: Reached its 496 km near-polar orbit; ATLAS first light 2018-09-30, science operations from late October.

costBuild.note: Grew from an original ~$500M estimate, largely due to the ATLAS instrument.

costLaunch.note: Delta II, NASA Launch Services.

satellites.status: Operational

purpose.summary: Measure ice-sheet and sea-ice elevation change plus vegetation canopy with photon-counting laser altimetry.

results.headline: Precise laser altimetry of Earth’s ice — how fast ice sheets and sea ice are changing.

bullets.text: Mapped Greenland and Antarctic elevation change at high resolution, quantifying ice loss contribution to sea level.
bullets.source: NASA ICESat-2 science team / Nature & GRL papers

bullets.text: Sea-ice freeboard and thickness products improve Arctic/Antarctic ice-volume estimates.
Unexpected strength in vegetation and inland-water height applications.

results.stillDoing: Ongoing ATLAS altimetry; products via NSIDC.

satellites.name: SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography)
satellites.operator: NASA · CNES (with CSA and UK Space Agency)
satellites.manufacturer: Thales Alenia Space (bus) · NASA JPL (KaRIn instrument)

built.text: Joint NASA–CNES development from 2009; completed 2022.

settled.text: Six-month calibration in a 1-day repeat orbit, then moved to the 21-day science orbit in July 2023.

costBuild.note: NASA share ~$1.1B; CNES contributed the bus and the Ka-band radar's RF unit.

costLaunch.note: NASA Launch Services contract with SpaceX, awarded 2016.

satellites.status: Operational

purpose.summary: Survey nearly all of Earth’s surface water — oceans and inland — with wide-swath Ka-band interferometry.

results.headline: First global high-resolution view of ocean eddies and continental surface water from one mission.

bullets.text: Early KaRIn maps resolved fine-scale ocean topography previously invisible to nadir altimeters.
Demonstrated simultaneous lake/river stage and floodplain observations for hydrology.

results.stillDoing: Cal/val and science phase; hydrology and ocean products rolling out via NASA/CNES.

satellites.name: Sentinel-1A
satellites.manufacturer: Thales Alenia Space Italy (prime) · Airbus DS (C-band SAR)

built.text: Copernicus first-generation radar satellite; completed 2013.

settled.text: Five-month commissioning; routine Copernicus service and free open data distribution from September 2014.

costBuild.note: Unit cost within the Sentinel-1 series contract.

costLaunch.note: Dedicated Soyuz from Kourou.

maintenance.note: The EU Copernicus programme's total budget is ~€5.8B for 2021–2027, covering all Sentinels, ground segment and data distribution.

satellites.status: Operational — its twin Sentinel-1B failed in December 2021 and was replaced by Sentinel-1C in 2024

purpose.summary: All-weather C-band radar imaging for Copernicus — land, ice, maritime, and emergency response.

results.headline: Workhorse open SAR for disasters, ice, and ground deformation worldwide.

bullets.text: Rapid mapping for floods, earthquakes, and volcanoes via the Copernicus Emergency Management Service.
Interferometry (InSAR) monitors subsidence, infrastructure, and tectonic strain at continental scale.
Maritime surveillance: ice charts and ship detection independent of clouds/night.
bullets.source: EUMETSAT / national ice services using S-1

results.stillDoing: Operational Copernicus SAR (constellation status varies as A/B/C units age/replace).

satellites.name: Sentinel-2A

built.text: Multispectral imager built by Airbus Spain; spacecraft completed 2015.

settled.text: Commissioning completed and routine operations declared; open data from December 2015.

costBuild.note: Series unit cost.

costLaunch.note: Vega.

maintenance.note: See Sentinel-1A.

satellites.status: Operational

purpose.summary: High-resolution multispectral optical imaging for land monitoring under Copernicus.

results.headline: Global 10–20 m optical workhorse — agriculture, forests, and land change at open-data scale.

bullets.text: With Sentinel-2B/C, ~5-day revisit enables crop monitoring and deforestation alerts worldwide.
Became a default input for commercial EO analytics alongside Landsat.

results.stillDoing: Operational multispectral land imaging; open data via Copernicus Data Space.

satellites.name: Suomi NPP

built.text: Originally the NPOESS Preparatory Project; completed 2011 after the NPOESS program was cancelled in 2010.

settled.text: Instrument checkout through early 2012; became the operational afternoon polar weather satellite.

costBuild.note: Absorbed sunk cost from the cancelled $13B NPOESS program.

costLaunch.note: Delta II.

maintenance.note: Operated inside the JPSS ground system — see NOAA-20.

satellites.status: Operational

purpose.summary: Bridge NOAA/NASA polar orbiter for weather and climate continuity after the POES/EOS era.

results.headline: First JPSS-pathfinder — VIIRS night lights and operational polar weather sounding.

bullets.text: VIIRS day/night band created a new standard for nighttime lights and disaster power-outage mapping.
CrIS/ATMS soundings feed global NWP models as part of the Joint Polar Satellite System backbone.

results.stillDoing: Aging but historically critical polar weather/climate observations.

satellites.name: NOAA-20 (JPSS-1)

built.text: First operational Joint Polar Satellite System spacecraft; completed 2017.

settled.text: Declared operational after a six-month validation campaign, flying 50 minutes ahead of Suomi NPP in the same orbital plane.

costBuild.note: Per-satellite share of the JPSS program.

costLaunch.note: Delta II under NASA Launch Services.

maintenance.note: NOAA's JPSS line covers satellites, ground system and operations. Lifecycle cost through 2038 is ~$11.3B.

satellites.status: Operational — primary US afternoon-orbit weather satellite

purpose.summary: Primary JPSS-1 polar satellite for operational weather forecasting and climate monitoring.

results.headline: Operational JPSS workhorse — critical input to global weather prediction.

bullets.text: ATMS/CrIS data assimilated into major NWP centers, improving medium-range forecast skill.
VIIRS continues fire, sea-surface, and night-lights products for civil agencies.

results.stillDoing: Operational polar weather satellite in the JPSS constellation.

satellites.name: GOES-16 (GOES-East, now on-orbit spare)

built.text: First of the GOES-R series; contract to Lockheed Martin in 2008, completed 2016.

settled.text: Drifted to 75.2°W and was declared the operational GOES-East after a 13-month checkout. Handed over to GOES-19 in April 2025 and moved to a standby slot.

costBuild.note: Per-satellite share. The GOES-R series total acquisition cost is ~$10.8B for four satellites plus ground system — roughly $2.7B each all-in.

costLaunch.note: Atlas V 541 under NASA Launch Services.

maintenance.note: NOAA's GOES-R operations line covers the whole constellation and its ground segment.

satellites.status: On-orbit spare at 104.7°W
sources: GAO-06-993 and follow-on GOES-R cost reports

purpose.summary: Geostationary weather satellite for the Americas — continuous imagery and severe-storm warning support.

results.headline: ABI and Geostationary Lightning Mapper remade Western Hemisphere weather monitoring.

bullets.text: ABI’s 16 bands and rapid scan improved hurricane, severe-storm, and fire monitoring cadence.
First operational geostationary lightning mapper (GLM) for the Americas.
Core of NWS forecasting and public weather imagery for CONUS and Atlantic tropics.

results.stillDoing: Operational GOES East (roles rotate with newer GOES-R series satellites).

satellites.name: GOES-19 (GOES-East)

built.text: Last of the four-satellite GOES-R series; completed 2024.

settled.text: Declared the operational GOES-East at 75.2°W after a ten-month post-launch test campaign.

costBuild.note: Per-satellite share of the ~$10.8B GOES-R series.

costLaunch.note: NASA Launch Services contract with SpaceX for a Falcon Heavy, awarded 2021.

satellites.status: Operational — primary US eastern weather satellite

purpose.summary: Newest GOES-R series geostationary weather satellite for the Americas.

results.headline: Results dossier not yet researched for this entry.

satellites.name: Himawari-8

built.text: Ordered 2009 alongside Himawari-9 under a combined build-and-operate PFI contract; completed 2014.

settled.text: Positioned at 140.7°E and began full operations, becoming the world's first operational geostationary satellite with a 16-band imager.

costBuild.note: Contracted as a bundled build + 15 years of operations for Himawari-8 and -9.

costLaunch.note: H-IIA 202.

maintenance.note: Japan procured operations as a service — Mitsubishi runs the ground segment for a fixed term.

satellites.status: Standby — handed primary duty to Himawari-9 in December 2022

purpose.summary: JMA geostationary weather satellite for East Asia and the Western Pacific.

results.headline: Results dossier not yet researched for this entry.

satellites.name: MetOp-C

built.text: Third of three MetOp satellites built as a single batch in the 2000s and stored until needed. Completed ~2006, stored 12 years.

settled.text: Commissioned into the morning polar orbit, briefly giving Europe three simultaneous MetOp satellites.

costBuild.note: Per-satellite share of the ~€2.4B EUMETSAT Polar System program for three satellites.

costLaunch.note: Soyuz from Kourou.

maintenance.note: EUMETSAT member-state contributions fund operations.

satellites.status: Operational — succeeded by the MetOp-SG series from 2025

purpose.summary: EUMETSAT polar orbiter for operational meteorology and climate sounding.

results.headline: Results dossier not yet researched for this entry.

satellites.name: GPS III (Navstar Block III)

built.text: Development contract awarded to Lockheed Martin in May 2008. First flight article completed 2017; satellites produced on a rolling line since.

launched.vehicle: Falcon 9 (GPS III SV01 'Vespucci'); later flights on Delta IV Medium, Falcon 9 and Vulcan

settled.text: SV01 was set healthy for civil use in January 2020 — 13 months after launch, an unusually long checkout because it was the first of a new block. Later units enter service in ~2–3 months.

costBuild.note: GAO put the first 10 GPS III satellites at ~$577M each including non-recurring development. The follow-on GPS IIIF program is $9.4B for 22 satellites — a program acquisition unit cost of ~$427M each.

costLaunch.note: SpaceX won GPS III launches at ~$83M; ULA Delta IV Medium flights cost roughly $150M. National-security launch pricing carries mission-assurance premiums.

maintenance.note: Covers constellation operations, sustainment and the ground segment. The OCX ground control program alone has cost over $7B and ran roughly eight years late.

satellites.status: Operational — 31 satellites usable across Blocks IIR, IIR-M, IIF and III
sources: GPS IIIF Selected Acquisition Report, December 2022 (DoD)
SpaceNews, GPS III cost growth reporting

purpose.summary: Next-generation US Global Positioning System satellites — more accurate, robust civil and military PNT.

results.headline: Underpins modern timing and navigation; GPS III upgrades accuracy, authenticity, and L1C for civil users.

bullets.text: GPS as a system enables global aviation, logistics, telecom timing, and precision agriculture — estimated economic value in the hundreds of billions of $/year in the US alone.
GPS III adds stronger civil L1C and improved anti-jam military M-code capability as vehicles enter the constellation.

results.stillDoing: Growing GPS III fraction of the operational GPS constellation (Space Force).

satellites.name: Galileo
satellites.operator: EUSPA (EU Agency for the Space Programme) · ESA
satellites.manufacturer: OHB System (bus) · SSTL (payload) for FOC; Airbus and Thales Alenia for Gen 2

built.text: In-Orbit Validation satellites built by Astrium/Thales from 2006. Full Operational Capability batches contracted to OHB from 2010 at roughly €40M per satellite.

launched.vehicle: Soyuz ST-B (first pair); later Ariane 5 ES quadruplets and Falcon 9

settled.text: Initial Services declared December 2016. Full Operational Capability was reached in 2024 with a 24-satellite operational constellation plus spares.

costBuild.note: OHB batch contracts. Total Galileo program cost including ground segment and EGNOS is roughly €10B through 2020.

costLaunch.note: Launched four at a time on Ariane 5 ES (~€120M) or in pairs on Soyuz. Two 2024 launches moved to Falcon 9 because Ariane 6 was late.

maintenance.note: EU allocated €9.0B to Galileo and EGNOS for 2021–2027 covering operations, replenishment and the second generation.

satellites.status: Operational — 24 usable satellites plus spares; Galileo Second Generation in development

purpose.summary: Europe’s independent global navigation satellite system for civil positioning, navigation, and timing.

results.headline: Operational EU GNSS — dual-frequency civil accuracy and European PNT autonomy.

bullets.text: Declared Initial Services in 2016; Open Service widely used in phones and receivers alongside GPS.
Search-and-rescue return-link and High Accuracy Service expand beyond basic GNSS.

results.stillDoing: Operational Galileo constellation under EU Space Programme (EUSPA).

satellites.name: BeiDou-3
satellites.operator: China Satellite Navigation Office · PLA Strategic Support Force
satellites.manufacturer: China Academy of Space Technology (CAST) · Shanghai Engineering Center for Microsatellites (SECM)

built.text: Third-generation design finalised ~2015; satellites produced in parallel batches at two manufacturers to sustain a launch every few weeks.

launched.vehicle: Long March 3B/YZ-1 (first BDS-3 pair); GEO and IGSO units on Long March 3B

settled.text: Formally commissioned by Xi Jinping on 2020-07-31, five weeks after the 30th and final core satellite launched — completing global coverage.

costBuild.note: China does not publish per-satellite costs. Chinese officials have cited roughly ¥120B (~$17B) for the entire three-generation BeiDou program from 1994.

costLaunch.note: BDS-3 deployment took ~30 launches over three years.

maintenance.note: Replenishment launches continue at a few per year.

satellites.status: Operational — 30+ satellites in a mixed MEO/IGSO/GEO architecture
sources: China Satellite Navigation Office white papers

purpose.summary: China’s global navigation satellite system for PNT services.

results.headline: Results dossier not yet researched for this entry.

satellites.name: GLONASS

built.text: Original constellation dates to 1982. GLONASS-M production ran 2003–2018; GLONASS-K from 2011 and GLONASS-K2 from 2023.

settled.text: The system first reached full 24-satellite coverage in 1995, collapsed to 6 working satellites by 2001 after the Soviet collapse, and was restored to full global coverage in December 2011.

costBuild.note: Russian figures are quoted in roubles across a period of large currency swings, so dollar conversions are unreliable. Federal GLONASS program funding was ~RUB 320B for 2012–2020.

costLaunch.note: Historically three at a time on Proton; now one at a time on Soyuz.

maintenance.note: Sanctions since 2022 have constrained access to radiation-hardened foreign components, slowing GLONASS-K2 production.

satellites.status: Operational — ~24–26 satellites, several past design life

purpose.summary: Russia’s global navigation satellite system.

results.headline: Results dossier not yet researched for this entry.

satellites.name: QZSS (Michibiki)

built.text: First satellite built by JAXA/MELCO from 2003; operational satellites from 2017.

settled.text: Four-satellite service started November 2018, giving Japan a GPS augmentation with at least one satellite near zenith over Tokyo at all times.

costBuild.note: Covers the first four satellites plus ground segment.

maintenance.note: Operated under a PFI service contract; expanding to 7 satellites.

satellites.status: Operational — expanding to a 7-satellite constellation
sources: Cabinet Office of Japan QZSS documentation

purpose.summary: Japan’s regional GNSS augmentation for the Asia-Oceania region.

satellites.name: Starlink

built.text: Announced 2015. Production reached ~5 satellites per day by 2023. Generations: v0.9 (2019), v1.0, v1.5 with laser links (2021), v2 mini (2023), v3 for Starship (2025).

launched.vehicle: Falcon 9 Block 5 — 60 at a time initially, now 20–28 v2 mini per flight

settled.text: Each satellite ion-thrusts from a ~300 km insertion orbit to its ~550 km operational shell over several weeks. Beta service opened October 2020; general availability October 2021.

costBuild.note: Elon Musk has stated v1.0 dropped under $250k–500k; the heavier 730 kg v2 mini is reported around $800k. SpaceX does not publish audited figures.

costLaunch.note: SpaceX launches its own satellites, so the relevant number is internal marginal cost — roughly $15–20M per reused Falcon 9 flight divided by ~23 satellites. The external Falcon 9 list price is $69.75M.

maintenance.note: Satellites are designed for ~5 years and then deorbited. Sustaining the constellation therefore requires roughly 2,000+ replacement satellites per year in perpetuity — an implied recurring cost on the order of $2B/yr in hardware alone. SpaceX has deorbited over 1,000 satellites to date.

satellites.status: Operational — the largest satellite constellation ever built, and roughly two-thirds of all active satellites
sources: Elon Musk public statements on unit cost
SpaceNews and Wikipedia 'List of Starlink launches' for cadence

purpose.summary: Low-Earth-orbit broadband constellation to deliver internet where fiber and cellular are scarce or contested.

results.headline: Largest satellite constellation ever — consumer and government broadband at scale.

bullets.text: Millions of users across 100+ countries; primary connectivity for many rural and maritime customers.
Became critical wartime and disaster connectivity (notably Ukraine and hurricane responses).
Drove industry and regulatory focus on mega-constellation debris, brightness, and spectrum.
bullets.source: FCC / IAU / NASA orbital debris discussions

results.stillDoing: Rapidly expanding LEO broadband; military/government variants (e.g. Starshield) alongside consumer service.

satellites.name: OneWeb (Eutelsat OneWeb)
satellites.manufacturer: Airbus OneWeb Satellites JV, Merritt Island, Florida

built.text: Purpose-built mass-production line opened 2019 with a target of 2 satellites per day — the first true assembly line for spacecraft.

launched.vehicle: Soyuz ST-B (34–36 at a time); after Russia seized 36 satellites in 2022, switched to Falcon 9, LVM3 and NewSpace India
launched.site: Kourou, Baikonur, Vostochny, Cape Canaveral, Sriharikota

settled.text: Constellation of 618 satellites completed March 2023; global commercial service phased in through 2024.

costBuild.note: Airbus targeted under $1M per satellite at volume — the figure that made the business case.

costLaunch.note: Roughly $60–70M per launch of ~36 satellites.

maintenance.note: OneWeb went bankrupt in March 2020 after raising $3.4B, was bought by the UK government and Bharti for $1B, and merged with Eutelsat in 2023. A second-generation constellation is planned.

satellites.status: Operational — 648 satellites

purpose.summary: LEO broadband constellation (Eutelsat OneWeb) for enterprise and government connectivity.

satellites.name: Iridium NEXT
satellites.manufacturer: Thales Alenia Space (design) · Northrop Grumman Innovation Systems, Gilbert, Arizona (assembly)

built.text: Contract to Thales Alenia signed 2010 to replace the original 1990s constellation; production ran 2015–2018.

settled.text: The final 10 satellites launched 2019-01-11 and the constellation was declared complete on 2019-02-05, replacing all 66 first-generation satellites one slot at a time without a service gap.

costBuild.note: $3B total for 81 satellites (66 operational, 9 on-orbit spares, 6 ground spares) including launch — Iridium's own published program figure.

costLaunch.note: Eight Falcon 9 launches at roughly $62M each, 10 satellites per flight.

maintenance.note: Iridium has publicly guided to low ongoing capex through the 2030s — the constellation is fully deployed and paid for. Reported in Iridium's SEC filings.

satellites.status: Operational — 66 active satellites plus spares; the only constellation with true global pole-to-pole coverage

purpose.summary: Global L-band voice and data constellation, including Iridium Certus broadband.

satellites.name: Intelsat 39

built.text: Ordered 2016 to replace Intelsat 902; completed 2019.

settled.text: Raised from geostationary transfer orbit to 62°E over about seven weeks, then entered commercial service.

costBuild.note: Typical SSL-1300 class GEO comsat. Intelsat does not disclose per-satellite prices.

costLaunch.note: Ariane 5 dual-launch slot; a full Ariane 5 ECA ran ~$150–180M.

maintenance.note: GEO satellites are cheap to operate once on station: station-keeping, a teleport, and a share of a control centre. The dominant cost was the capital spend.

satellites.status: Operational at 62°E

purpose.summary: Geostationary communications satellite for media, mobility, and network services.

satellites.name: SES-17

built.text: Ordered 2016 for in-flight connectivity over the Americas; completed 2021 after COVID delays.

settled.text: All-electric propulsion meant a slow spiral — about six months to climb from transfer orbit to its 67.1°W slot. Commercial service began June 2022.

costBuild.note: A very-high-throughput satellite with ~200 spot beams and a digital transparent processor — several times the cost of a conventional GEO comsat.

satellites.status: Operational at 67.1°W

purpose.summary: High-throughput Ka-band GEO satellite for aviation, maritime, and enterprise.

satellites.name: ViaSat-3 Americas (F1)

built.text: Program announced 2016; first satellite completed 2023 after repeated delays.

settled.text: Never fully commissioned. The main reflector antenna failed to deploy in July 2023, leaving the satellite at under 10% of its intended ~1 Tbps capacity. It was repositioned and is used in a degraded role.

costBuild.note: Viasat has described the three-satellite ViaSat-3 program as roughly $2B in total capital.

costLaunch.note: Expendable Falcon Heavy.

maintenance.note: The clearest public example of what a satellite failure actually costs. Viasat recorded a $420M insurance recovery and the third ViaSat-3 was re-planned around the loss.

satellites.status: Degraded — antenna deployment failure, operating at a fraction of design capacity
sources: Viasat SEC filings and investor calls, 2023–2024
SpaceNews coverage of the ViaSat-3 anomaly

purpose.summary: Ultra-high-capacity GEO broadband satellite for the Americas.

satellites.name: TDRS-13 (TDRS-M)

built.text: Third of the third-generation TDRS satellites; completed 2017. An omni antenna was damaged during pre-launch processing and had to be replaced.

settled.text: Placed into the on-orbit spare fleet after checkout. TDRS is the relay network that carries ISS and Hubble traffic to the ground.

costBuild.note: Total mission cost including launch was ~$408M.

costLaunch.note: NASA Launch Services contract with ULA.

maintenance.note: NASA's Space Communications and Navigation budget for the TDRS constellation and its ground terminals at White Sands and Guam. NASA is transitioning to buying commercial relay services instead of replacing TDRS.

satellites.status: Operational — final TDRS ever built; no successors planned

purpose.summary: NASA Tracking and Data Relay Satellite for near-continuous LEO spacecraft communications.

satellites.name: AEHF-6

built.text: Sixth and final Advanced Extremely High Frequency satellite; completed 2020.

launched.site: Cape Canaveral, Florida — the first launch for the newly created Space Force

settled.text: Used both chemical and electric propulsion to reach geostationary orbit over roughly six months, then entered the protected-communications constellation.

costBuild.note: Per-satellite share. The AEHF program total is roughly $15B for six satellites plus terminals and ground segment.

costLaunch.note: Atlas V 551 under the EELV/NSSL program — national-security launches cost substantially more than commercial equivalents.

maintenance.note: Operations are funded inside classified and unclassified Space Force lines that are not broken out per satellite.

satellites.status: Operational — provides nuclear-survivable, jam-resistant comms for US and allied forces
sources: US Space Force / SSC press releases

purpose.summary: US protected strategic military communications in GEO.

satellites.name: SBIRS GEO-1
satellites.manufacturer: Lockheed Martin (A2100 bus) · Northrop Grumman (infrared sensors)

built.text: SBIRS was contracted in 1996 and became one of the most troubled US space programs — the first satellite was delivered roughly nine years late.

settled.text: Extended checkout of the scanning and staring infrared sensors; entered operational missile-warning service in 2013.

costBuild.note: Per-satellite share of a ~$19B program for 6 GEO satellites and 4 hosted HEO payloads. Original 1996 estimate for the whole program was $4B.

costLaunch.note: Atlas V 401 under EELV.

maintenance.note: Being succeeded by Next-Gen OPIR, itself budgeted at ~$14B.

satellites.status: Operational — strategic missile early warning

purpose.summary: US Space Force missile-warning satellite — detect and characterize ballistic missile launches from GEO.

results.headline: Operational missile-warning layer; detailed performance is classified.

bullets.text: Part of SBIRS, which replaced DSP for US strategic missile warning and battlespace awareness.
Specific detection statistics and tactical outcomes are not publicly released.

results.stillDoing: On-orbit missile warning; being succeeded over time by Next-Gen OPIR.

satellites.name: MUOS-5

built.text: Fifth Mobile User Objective System satellite, built as the on-orbit spare; completed 2016.

settled.text: An orbit-raising thruster failed on 2016-06-29, stranding it short of its slot. Engineers used the backup propulsion to complete the climb over seven months and it reached its test slot in early 2017.

costBuild.note: Per-satellite share of a ~$7.7B program for five satellites and the ground system.

costLaunch.note: Atlas V 551.

satellites.status: Operational as an on-orbit spare — a good example of a $1.5B asset nearly lost to a single thruster

purpose.summary: US Navy narrowband military UHF SATCOM (Mobile User Objective System).

satellites.name: WGS-1 (Wideband Global SATCOM)

built.text: First of the WGS series replacing the Defense Satellite Communications System; completed 2007.

settled.text: Entered service over the Pacific in April 2008.

costBuild.note: WGS program is roughly $5B for 11 satellites. Australia funded WGS-6 outright (~$707M) in exchange for constellation access — a rare published per-satellite figure.

satellites.name: Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich

built.text: Built as a pair (6A and 6B) under a joint transatlantic agreement; 6A completed 2020.

settled.text: Flew 30 seconds behind Jason-3 for six months of cross-calibration, then took over as the reference sea-level mission in June 2021 — continuing an unbroken record that began with TOPEX/Poseidon in 1992.

costBuild.note: Costs split across five agencies, which makes a single figure approximate.

costLaunch.note: NASA Launch Services contract with SpaceX, awarded 2017.

maintenance.note: EUMETSAT operates the spacecraft; NASA and NOAA fund instruments and data processing.

satellites.status: Operational — Sentinel-6B launched 2025 to continue the series

purpose.summary: Reference sea-level altimetry mission continuing the TOPEX/Jason climate record (Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich).

results.headline: Extends the gold-standard global sea-level rise record into the 2020s.

bullets.text: Continues the uninterrupted altimetry climate data record begun by TOPEX/Poseidon (1992).
Provides the reference orbit for calibrating other altimeters and ocean models.

results.stillDoing: Operational reference altimetry; twin Sentinel-6B planned for continuity.

satellites.name: Jason-3

built.text: Fourth in the TOPEX/Jason ocean altimetry lineage; completed 2015.

launched.vehicle: Falcon 9 v1.1 — the final flight of that variant

settled.text: Took over the reference orbit from Jason-2 after several months of tandem flight and cross-calibration.

costBuild.note: Shared across four agencies.

costLaunch.note: NASA Launch Services contract with SpaceX.

maintenance.note: Now an interleaved backup to Sentinel-6.

satellites.status: Operational in a drifting/interleaved orbit

purpose.summary: Precision ocean altimeter bridging Jason-2 and Sentinel-6 for sea-level and ocean circulation.

results.headline: Key mid-2010s link in the global sea-level rise time series.

bullets.text: Extended precise sea-level and mesoscale ocean topography used in climate assessments.
Cross-calibrated the transition toward Sentinel-6 as the new reference altimeter.

results.stillDoing: Extended mission / climate record support alongside Sentinel-6.

satellites.name: SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive)

built.text: Decadal Survey mission; completed 2014 with a 6-metre deployable mesh reflector.

settled.text: Reflector spun up and both instruments commissioned by May 2015. The radar failed permanently on 2015-07-07 after ten weeks; the radiometer continues to operate.

costBuild.note: Total mission cost ~$916M including launch and operations.

costLaunch.note: Delta II.

satellites.status: Partially operational — radar failed 2015, radiometer still returning data

purpose.summary: Map global soil moisture and freeze/thaw state for weather, drought, and carbon-cycle science.

results.headline: Global L-band soil moisture — drought, flood, and NWP applications despite early radar loss.

bullets.text: Radiometer-only mission after radar failure still delivered validated global soil-moisture products.
Products used in drought monitoring, agriculture, and assimilation into land-surface / weather models.

results.stillDoing: Ongoing radiometer soil-moisture and freeze/thaw data.

satellites.name: GPM Core Observatory

built.text: Successor to TRMM; completed 2013.

settled.text: Commissioned into a 65° inclined 407 km orbit, anchoring a constellation of partner satellites that together map global precipitation every 30 minutes.

costBuild.note: NASA lifecycle cost; JAXA provided the radar and the launch.

costLaunch.note: JAXA contributed the H-IIA launch in exchange for the radar partnership — an in-kind trade rather than a cash cost.

satellites.status: Operational

purpose.summary: International precipitation-measuring mission — rain and snowfall for weather, climate, and disasters.

results.headline: Global standard for spaceborne rain and snow measurement after TRMM.

bullets.text: Dual-frequency radar + microwave imager improved light rain and snowfall detection vs TRMM.
IMERG and related products used worldwide for floods, landslides, and climate precipitation datasets.

results.stillDoing: Core observatory plus constellation partners; precipitation products via NASA PPS.

satellites.name: GRACE-FO 1
satellites.operator: NASA · GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences

built.text: Twin satellites that measure Earth's gravity field by tracking the distance between each other to within a micron; completed 2017.

launched.vehicle: Falcon 9 Block 4 (rideshare with 5 Iridium NEXT satellites)

settled.text: Formation established at ~220 km separation; science operations from late 2018 after a microwave instrument processor swap.

costBuild.note: NASA cost; Germany contributed the launch share and ground segment.

costLaunch.note: Sharing a Falcon 9 with Iridium made this one of the cheapest launches for a flagship-adjacent science mission.

satellites.status: Operational

purpose.summary: Track month-to-month changes in Earth’s gravity field to map water mass movement.

results.headline: Continues the GRACE record of melting ice and shrinking groundwater from space.

bullets.text: With GRACE (2002–2017), revealed groundwater depletion in aquifers from California to India.
Quantifies ice-sheet and glacier mass loss contribution to sea-level rise.
Laser ranging interferometer demonstrated finer inter-satellite ranging for future gravity missions.

results.stillDoing: Monthly gravity-field and mass-change products via NASA/GFZ/JPL.

satellites.name: Planet Labs Dove / SuperDove

built.text: 3U cubesats built in-house on an iterative 'agile aerospace' model — roughly 15 hardware generations since 2013, each flown before the next is finalised.

launched.vehicle: Rideshare on almost everything: Antares, Falcon 9 Transporter, PSLV, Electron, and deployed from the ISS

settled.text: Reached a 'daily global scan' capability in 2017 with ~150 satellites — the first constellation to image the entire land surface of Earth every day.

costBuild.note: Planet does not publish unit cost, but the model depends on the satellites being cheap and disposable rather than exquisite.

costLaunch.note: SpaceX Transporter rideshare is priced around $6,000/kg; a 5 kg Dove is a very small share of a launch.

maintenance.note: Doves have no propulsion and deorbit naturally in 3–5 years. Planet has launched over 500 and treats attrition as normal.

satellites.status: Operational — the largest Earth-imaging constellation

purpose.summary: Fleet of optical Earth-imaging CubeSats for daily global monitoring.

satellites.name: Vanguard 1

built.text: Built at NRL in 1957–58 as a 1.47 kg grapefruit-sized test sphere. Khrushchev called it 'the grapefruit satellite'.

settled.text: The fourth satellite ever launched, and the first to use solar cells.

costBuild.note: The whole Project Vanguard program in then-year dollars — roughly $1.2B today. The satellite itself was a tiny fraction of that.

maintenance.note: It stopped transmitting in 1964 and has been an inert object ever since. Nobody pays anything to keep it there.

satellites.status: Derelict — but the oldest human-made object still in orbit, and expected to stay up for another ~180 years

purpose.summary: Early US naval research satellite — test launch vehicle, miniaturization, and geodesy from orbit.

results.headline: Oldest human-made object still in orbit — and an early win for space-based geodesy.

bullets.text: Proved solar-powered miniaturized satellites could survive long-term in orbit (launched 1958).
Tracking data helped refine Earth’s shape (oblateness) and atmospheric density models.
Remains in orbit as a derelict — a monument to the first years of the Space Age.

results.stillDoing: Inactive; tracked as debris/derelict for catalog and historical interest.
